## Q1
In a \_\_\_\_ the left and right subtrees for any given node, differ in height by more than one.

## Q1 - Options
(A) Balanced Binary Tree
(B) Weight balanced binary tree
(C) Height balanced tree
(D) Binary Search Tree

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q25

As printed, the stem describes a height imbalance of more than one level, but every option listed here, balanced binary tree, weight balanced tree, height balanced tree, and binary search tree, actually names a tree property that either requires balance or says nothing about height difference at all, so none of them literally matches a subtree height gap greater than one.

A height balanced (AVL) tree is specifically defined by the opposite condition, that every node's left and right subtree heights differ by at most one, which is almost certainly what this stem intended to describe before an OCR or transcription error inverted "at most" into "more than."

Because the printed condition does not correspond to any option's actual definition, this question has no option that is correct as literally worded, which is consistent with the source noting that NTA dropped this item from the final answer key. The closest intended concept, once the wording is corrected to "differ by at most one," is the height balanced tree.

## Q2
Consider the following statements:

A. The number of labelled binary trees possible with 'n' nodes is (2n)!/(n+1)!<br>
B. The number of binary search trees possible with 'n' nodes is (2n)!/((n+1)!n!)<br>
C. The number of unlabeled binary trees possible with 'n' nodes is C(2n,n)/(n+1)!<br>
D. The number of simple, undirected and labelled graphs possible with 'n' vertices is 2^(n(n-1)/2)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q2 - Options
(A) A, B and C are only correct
(B) A, B and D are only correct
(C) B, C and D are only correct
(D) A, C and D are only correct

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q41

The number of unlabeled (shape-only) binary trees with n nodes equals the Catalan number Cₙ = C(2n,n)/(n+1), dividing by (n+1) and not by (n+1)!

Statement C instead writes the denominator as (n+1)!, an extra factorial that changes the value for any n&gt;0, so C is false as printed.

- **A.** Labelled binary trees are formed by taking each of the Cₙ possible shapes and assigning n distinct labels to its nodes in n! ways, giving Cₙ·n! = [(2n)!/(n!(n+1)!)]·n! = (2n)!/(n+1)!. True.
- **B.** A binary search tree's shape is uniquely determined once n distinct keys are fixed, so the number of BSTs equals the number of possible shapes, the Catalan number Cₙ = (2n)!/((n+1)!n!). True.
- **D.** A simple undirected graph on n labelled vertices is determined by choosing a subset of its C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 possible edges, giving 2^(n(n-1)/2) distinct labelled graphs. True.

Since A, B, and D hold while C contains the factorial error, the correct option is A, B and D are only correct.

## Q3
Which of the following rotations are correctly explained in the context of an AVL tree.

A. LL rotation: The new node is inserted in the left sub-tree of the left sub-tree of the critical node.<br>
B. RR rotation: The new node is inserted in the right sub-tree of the right sub-tree of the critical node.<br>
C. LR rotation: The new node is inserted in the right sub-tree of the left sub-tree of the critical node.<br>
D. RL rotation: The new node is inserted in the left sub-tree of the right sub-tree of the critical node

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

## Q3 - Options
(A) A, D only
(B) A, C Only
(C) A, B Only
(D) B, C Only

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (15 Mar, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q55

Each of the four statements matches the standard textbook description of when its named AVL rotation applies.

An LL imbalance occurs when the new node lands in the left subtree of the left child of the critical node, exactly as statement A describes, and an RR imbalance occurs symmetrically when it lands in the right subtree of the right child, as statement B describes.

An LR imbalance occurs when the new node lands in the right subtree of the left child (statement C), and an RL imbalance occurs when it lands in the left subtree of the right child (statement D). All four descriptions are individually accurate by the standard definition of these four rotation cases, so no two-item combination among the given options can capture all of them correctly. This mismatch between four true statements and answer choices offering only two at a time is consistent with this item being dropped from the final NTA answer key, and no single pair should be treated as more "correct" than the others.

## Q4
The number of nodes of height h in any n-element heap is atmost:

## Q4 - Options
(A) n / 2^(h+1)
(B) n / 2^(h−1)
(C) n / 2^h
(D) (n−1) / 2^(h−1)

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q44

In a binary heap stored as a nearly-complete binary tree, the standard bound states that the number of nodes at height h is at most ⌈n / 2^(h+1)⌉, since each level roughly halves the count of nodes above it and height-h nodes sit h levels above the leaves. This matches option A, n / 2^(h+1).

## Q5
Consider a B-tree of height h, minimum degree t ≥ 2 that contains any n-key, where n ≥ 1. Which of the following is correct?

## Q5 - Options
(A) h ≥ log ((n+1)/2) ₜ
(B) h ≤ log ((n+1)/2) ₜ
(C) h ≥ log ((n−1)/2) ₜ
(D) h ≤ log ((n−1)/2) ₜ

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q45

For a B-tree of minimum degree t holding n keys, the standard height bound (derived from the minimum number of keys a tree of height h must hold once every non-root node is at its minimum fill) gives

h ≤ log_t((n+1)/2)

This is the upper bound on height guaranteed by the B-tree's minimum branching factor, matching option B.

## Q6
Consider the traversal of a tree<br>
Preorder → ABCEIFJDGHKL<br>
Inorder → EICFJBGDKHLA<br>
Which of the following is correct post order traversal?

## Q6 - Options
(A) EIFJCKGLHDBA
(B) FCGKLHDBUAE
(C) FCGKLHDBAEIJ
(D) IEJFCGKLHDBA

## Q6 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q48

Rebuild the tree recursively from preorder and inorder. A is the root since it is the first preorder symbol, and since A is the very last symbol in the inorder sequence, A has no right subtree, everything else falls under its left child B.

Splitting B's inorder region (EICFJBGDKHL) around B gives a left part EICFJ and a right part GDKHL, matching the next preorder symbols C,E,I,F,J for the left and D,G,H,K,L for the right.

Working through each smaller region the same way places C with left child E (E has right child I) and right child F (F has right child J), and places D with left child G and right child H (H has left child K and right child L).

Walking this reconstructed tree in left, right, root order gives

I, E, J, F, C, G, K, L, H, D, B, A

which is IEJFCGKLHDBA.

## Q7
How many rotations are required during the construction of an AVL tree if the following elements are to be added in the given sequence?<br>
35, 50, 40, 25, 30, 60, 78, 20, 28

## Q7 - Options
(A) 2 left rotations, 2 right rotations
(B) 2 left rotations, 3 right rotations
(C) 3 left rotations, 2 right rotations
(D) 3 left rotations, 1 right rotation

## Q7 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q49

Insert each key and rebalance as soon as any node's balance factor exceeds 1.

Inserting 40 after 35, 50 creates a Right-Left imbalance at 35, fixed with a right rotation at 50 followed by a left rotation at 35 (40 becomes the new subtree root).

Inserting 30 after 25 creates a Left-Right imbalance at 35 (now under 40), fixed with a left rotation at 25 followed by a right rotation at 35 (30 becomes the new subtree root).

Inserting 78 after 60 creates a Right-Right imbalance at 50, fixed with a single left rotation at 50.

Inserting 20 and 28 afterward keeps every node balanced with no further rotations.

Counting individual rotations across the two double rotations and one single rotation gives 3 left rotations and 2 right rotations in total.

## Q8
Two balanced binary search trees hold m and n elements respectively. They can be merged into one balanced binary search tree in \_\_\_\_\_\_ time.

## Q8 - Options
(A) O(m\*n)
(B) O(m + n)
(C) O(m\*log n)
(D) O(m\*log(m + n))

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q43

In-order traversal of each tree yields a sorted list in O(m) and O(n). Merge the two sorted lists in O(m + n), then build a balanced BST from the merged array in O(m + n). Total O(m + n).

## Q9
A data structure must store a set of integers so that each of the following runs in O(log n) time: delete the smallest element, and insert an element only if it is not already present. Which structure can be used?

## Q9 - Options
(A) A heap can be used but not a balanced binary search tree
(B) A balanced binary search tree can be used but not a heap
(C) Both a balanced binary search tree and a heap can be used
(D) Neither a balanced binary search tree nor a heap can be used

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q44

A balanced BST supports find-min, delete-min, membership test and insert all in O(log n). A min-heap gives O(log n) delete-min, but checking whether a value is already present needs an O(n) scan, so it cannot do the conditional insert in O(log n).

## Q10
The order of a leaf node in a B+ tree is the maximum number of (value, data-record-pointer) pairs it can hold. Given block size 1 KB (1024 bytes), data-record pointer 7 bytes, value field 9 bytes, and block pointer 6 bytes, what is the order of the leaf node?

## Q10 - Options
(A) 63
(B) 64
(C) 67
(D) 68

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q48

A B+ tree leaf holds m (value + record-pointer) pairs plus one block pointer to the next leaf: m x (9 + 7) + 6 &lt;= 1024, so 16m &lt;= 1018, m &lt;= 63.6. The order is 63.

## Q11
A B-tree indexes a database file. Search-key field = 10 bytes, block size = 1024 bytes, record pointer = 9 bytes, block pointer = 8 bytes. Let K be the order of an internal node and L the order of a leaf node. Then (K, L) = \_\_\_\_\_\_.

## Q11 - Options
(A) (57, 53)
(B) (50, 52)
(C) (60, 64)
(D) (34, 31)

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2021 (26 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q66

Internal node: K block pointers and K-1 keys fit in a block: 8K + 10(K - 1) &lt;= 1024, so 18K &lt;= 1034, K = 57. Leaf node: L (key + record-pointer) entries plus one block pointer: 19L + 8 &lt;= 1024, so 19L &lt;= 1016, L = 53.

## Q12
In a binary max heap containing n numbers, the smallest element can be found in what time?

## Q12 - Options
(A) O(n)
(B) O(log₂ n)
(C) O(1)
(D) O(log log n)

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Nov 2020 (11 Nov, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q24

A max heap only guarantees that the largest element is at the root. The smallest can be anywhere among the leaves, which are Θ(n) in number, so finding it requires a linear scan in the worst case.

## Q13
In a B-Tree, each node represents a disk block. Suppose one block holds 8192 bytes. Each key uses 32 bytes. In a B-tree of order M there are M - 1 keys. Since each branch is on another disk block, we assume a branch is of 4 bytes. The total memory requirement for a non-leaf node is:

## Q13 - Options
(A) 32M - 32
(B) 36M - 32
(C) 36M - 36
(D) 32M - 36

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q32

In a B-tree of order M, a non-leaf node holds at most M - 1 keys and M branch pointers:

1. Memory for keys:<br>
   (M - 1) × 32 bytes = 32M - 32 bytes
2. Memory for branch pointers:<br>
   M × 4 bytes = 4M bytes

Total memory requirement:<br>
Total = (32M - 32) + 4M = 36M - 32 bytes

## Q14
The elements 42, 25, 30, 40, 22, 35, 26 are inserted one by one in the given order into a max-heap. The resultant max-heap is stored in an array implementation as

## Q14 - Options
(A) &lt;42, 35, 40, 22, 25, 26, 30&gt;
(B) &lt;42, 35, 40, 22, 25, 30, 26&gt;
(C) &lt;42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 26, 30&gt;
(D) &lt;42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 30, 26&gt;

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q57

Simulating one-by-one max-heap insertion with bottom-up percolation produces array &lt;42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 30, 26&gt;.

1. Insert 42: [42]
2. Insert 25: [42, 25]
3. Insert 30: [42, 25, 30]
4. Insert 40: Placed at index 4 (child of 25). Since 40 &gt; 25, swap 40 and 25 -&gt; [42, 40, 30, 25]
5. Insert 22: Placed at index 5 (child of 40). 22 &lt; 40, no swap -&gt; [42, 40, 30, 25, 22]
6. Insert 35: Placed at index 6 (child of 30). Since 35 &gt; 30, swap 35 and 30 -&gt; [42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 30]
7. Insert 26: Placed at index 7 (child of 35). 26 &lt; 35, no swap -&gt; [42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 30, 26]

- The resulting heap array is &lt;42, 40, 35, 25, 22, 30, 26&gt; (Option D).

## Q15
A binary search tree is constructed by inserting the following numbers in order :

60, 25, 72, 15, 30, 68, 101, 13, 18, 47, 70, 34

The number of nodes is the left subtree is

## Q15 - Options
(A) 3
(B) 7
(C) 5
(D) 6

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Trees: BST, AVL & Heaps
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q59

In a binary search tree, all elements strictly less than the root value reside in its left subtree.

- The root is the first inserted key, which is 60.
- Scanning the remaining sequence for values strictly less than 60:<br>
    25 (&lt; 60)<br>
    15 (&lt; 60)<br>
    30 (&lt; 60)<br>
    13 (&lt; 60)<br>
    18 (&lt; 60)<br>
    47 (&lt; 60)<br>
    34 (&lt; 60)
- There are exactly 7 elements less than 60 (25, 15, 30, 13, 18, 47, 34).
- The remaining elements (72, 68, 101, 70) are greater than 60 and enter the right subtree.
- Therefore, the left subtree contains 7 nodes (Option B).
